source_locator.description: Opening bracketed direction immediately after the canonical scene-1 heading.

translation.english_text: (The lawyer is speaking.)

The report in the newspapers saying that Poomalai committed the murder is false! After the investigation, the very shape of the case has changed. There is no basic reason at all why Poomalai should have killed the murdered man. (Poomalai is shown.) From the very beginning, Pandiyan has been the murdered man's bitterest enemy. (Pandiyan is shown.) In family matters and in public life alike, hostility has been growing between the two for many days. That hostility turned into hatred and ended in murder!
notes: Personal names are transliterated in the English text; the exact Tamil speaker label remains immutable metadata.
The two source-visible display directions embedded in the lawyer's utterance remain inside this dialogue unit.

translation.english_text: No. Pandiyan is innocent! He did not commit the murder—did not commit the murder. I alone committed the murder.
notes: The source repeats the denial across the dash; the English deliberately preserves that repetition rather than smoothing it away.

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical between Poomalai's first admission and the lawyer's response.

translation.english_text: (The judge bangs the table. Silence.)
notes: The source itself uses the English word `Silence`; it is retained in meaning rather than treated as an editorial insertion.

translation.english_text: Poomalai is taking the murder charge upon herself because of her affection for Pandiyan—for the sole reason that she does not want to give Pandiyan away.
No, no. Your Honour! Pandiyan has nothing whatsoever to do with this murder. Please listen to my entire family history!......
notes: The emphatic repeated `இல்லை இல்லை` and the extended source ellipsis are preserved rather than reduced to a single denial.

translation.english_text: What connection is there between this murder case and your family history?
notes: The conversational feminine address embedded in `என்னம்மா` is not expanded into an invented English name or title.

translation.english_text: There is a great deal! In support of this case, there is not only that history; there are also witnesses—the hospital watchman, the mill owner and others. Question them too! First listen to my story!

english_page_segments.english_text: There is a great deal! In support of this case, there is not only that history; there are also witnesses—the hospital watchman, the mill
owner and others. Question them too! First listen to my story!

notes: This cross-page dialogue mirrors the source break inside `மில் / முதலாளி`; the combined English restores the natural phrase `mill owner`.

translation.english_text: Tell me!...
Our family lived in Coimbatore! There was a bookshop there! Its name was Garudan Publishing House. It was there!...
notes: The corrected Tamil source reads `கோயமுத்தூர்`; the English uses the standard English toponym `Coimbatore`.
The unfinished source pivot `அங்கேதான்!...` is kept unfinished rather than completed with inferred narrative.

source_locator.description: Opening bracketed direction immediately after the canonical scene-2 heading.

translation.english_text: (Poomalai is teaching seven or eight children moral lessons through song.)
notes: The booklet prints only the performance reference; no song title or lyric body is supplied or reconstructed.

translation.english_text: You must come tomorrow morning...

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical after Poomalai dismisses the children.

translation.english_text: (The children leave.)
(Coming in with the drowsiness of someone just awakened) Yes, come in the morning! Then you can shout away without letting a man sleep...
You call this shouting? A child's prattle is sweeter than sugar candy!
Akka! I don't like any of this! Why do you call all these famine-stricken people here? Let them go to some charity school somewhere...
notes: `தர்மப் பள்ளிக்கூடம்` is retained as the source's charity-school reference rather than reduced to an unspecified school.

translation.english_text: I need something to pass the time, brother!
Are there no ways for women of rich households to pass the time? There are plenty! Badminton, ping-pong, ladies' club, English pictures—so many entertainments.
notes: The source's English code-switching is retained in meaning and register.

translation.english_text: There may be many ways, brother! But shouldn't it be useful to others too?
All right...your wish! From now on, even coming to this house just to sleep is a mistake! Aren't there choultries and rest houses for me?
notes: The earlier English incorrectly turned this first-person complaint into an instruction not to let other people sleep at the house. The corrected Tamil is about Paranthaman himself coming home merely to sleep.

translation.english_text: Brother, don't say things like that! We have a house as vast as the sea!
Fine, keep it that way! Akka! What is money for...to enjoy—life, pleasure, money—all are three-letter words.
notes: The source makes a Tamil word-length play; the English keeps the explicit claim rather than replacing it with a new English pun.

translation.english_text: Love, service—those too are three-letter words, Paranthama. Life is necessary, yes. But a life lived for others—that is the life one needs; pleasure is desirable—the pleasure of the heart that arises from other people's happiness.... ... ...
notes: The Tamil word-length contrast is preserved as a stated rhetorical device rather than recreated with different English vocabulary.

translation.english_text: Hmm. At this rate, this house will soon become an ashram.

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical after Paranthaman's ashram remark.

translation.english_text: (He leaves irritably. Bama's parents arrive.)
Who is it... ... Oh... ... come, come! Sit down! Gundumani! Bring tea!
notes: The exact Tamil label remains immutable metadata; the English uses a transliteration only in translated speech.

source_locator.description: Final parenthetical after Poomalai invites Bama's parents to sit.

translation.english_text: (Everyone sits down.)

source_locator.description: Opening bracketed direction immediately after the canonical scene-3 heading.

translation.english_text: (After putting down the toothbrush, he mutters to himself.)
Love...service...broad beans...
notes: The muttered source turns the preceding three-letter-word rhetoric into comic word association; `அவரைக்காய்` is translated literally as `broad beans` rather than replaced with a new English pun.

source_locator.description: Parenthetical between Paranthaman's muttering and his final line.

translation.english_text: (Angrily he turns the tap and takes a shower. Only after the water falls on him does it become clear that he is bathing without taking off his nightdress.)
notes: The source's English loanword `Nightdress` is translated as ordinary English without adding costume detail.

translation.english_text: Oh no! This is another nuisance.

source_locator.description: Opening bracketed direction immediately after the canonical scene-4 heading.

translation.english_text: (A woman carries away the used cups and saucers.)
Then I'm happy. The seventh is an auspicious day... ... ...
What does it matter what day it is!
No, madam! I have a little faith in auspicious days and stars.
notes: `நாள் நக்ஷத்திரம்` is retained as the source's paired astrological reference to day and star rather than reduced to stars alone.

translation.english_text: All right, all right... ... so what!
Why haven't you married, dear... ... ...

I'm the one responsible for this family, aren't I? My younger brother was brought up in comfort; Father and Mother ordered that the family's hardships should not be placed on him. My elder sister's daughter, who has no father or mother, is studying in Madras; I am her support.
notes: `சென்னை` is rendered as `Madras` in this 1953-period English derivative; the canonical Tamil remains unchanged.

translation.english_text: It is because you stand by everyone like a mother that they are looking for a life-partner for you who will live here with the household!...... ...
notes: The source refers to a husband who would remain in Poomalai's household; no modern family-law terminology is added.

translation.english_text: Oh dear...you won't find a husband like that... the girl is like Lakshmi herself!
notes: The source comparison to `லக்ஷிமி` is translated without normalizing the Tamil record.

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical before Poomalai introduces Bama's parents.

translation.english_text: (Paranthaman enters, bathed and dressed.)
Come, brother! Do you know these people? (Paranthaman stares blankly.) Oh! Looks as though you know only their daughter... ... Bama's parents!.
notes: The embedded source action remains inside the dialogue unit because it is part of the immutable dialogue record.

translation.english_text: Oh! Greetings!
They've come to settle the marriage! Well... ... you agree, don't you... ... ...

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical after Poomalai asks for Paranthaman's consent.

translation.english_text: (Paranthaman is silent, bashful.)
Why even ask him that! Is there a child who says it doesn't want a banana?
notes: The earlier English introduced extra broken wording not present in the corrected Tamil; this unit now follows the complete source sentence.

translation.english_text: What do you say, Paranthama!
All right, Akka!
Then it's settled. We'll be going. I'm happy. We'll attend to what has to be done.

source_locator.description: Opening bracketed direction immediately after the canonical scene-5 heading.

translation.english_text: (The sound 'tak, tak' is heard as the publishing-house rubber stamp is pressed onto tied parcels and book-post packets.)
notes: The source's sound effect is retained rather than replaced with an invented effect.

translation.english_text: (To the office boy) Boy...hmm...it's time for the parcels. Go...go. We can send the rest tomorrow.

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical sound cue after Garudan sends the boy off.

translation.english_text: ('Tak, tak'—the stamping sound.)
Who is it? Come in.

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical immediately after Garudan asks the visitor to enter.

translation.english_text: (Pandiyan comes in.)
Who are you...I feel I've seen you somewhere.... (suspiciously)
(Angrily) You may have forgotten. I am Pandiyan. Do you remember? (Showing the book in his hand) The true author of this book......
notes: The source prints `உண்மையான ஆசிரியர்......`; the printed dots are carried into the English so the broken-off utterance stays visible, matching how unfinished utterances are rendered elsewhere in this edition. An earlier note wrongly said the source had no ellipsis here.

translation.english_text: No, no...but the cover says the author is Paranthaman!

What does the printing machine know of the injustice you commit? I am the one who thought and thought, turned all my red blood into sweat, bore the hardship and laboured for many days to write it—wouldn't I know who wrote it?
notes: The source's bodily metaphor is preserved rather than softened.

translation.english_text: No—Paranthaman.
notes: The terse corrected source `இல்லை பரந்தாமன்.` is preserved rather than expanded into the earlier unsupported `Here is Paranthaman.`

translation.english_text: Who is this Paranthaman?
Devotee!
notes: The corrected exact source label is `குரல்` (voice), replacing the old derivative's `குரு`; the dialogue metadata now follows the corrected immutable record.

translation.english_text: Why are you angry? Why are you agitated—what is the matter for which you called Paranthaman? Who is this man?
He says he's Pandiyan.
Who is he! Pandiyan—the Pandiyan who won the battle of Thalaiyalanganam? Nedunchezhiyan who crossed the Aryan army? You Pandiyan who entered without any weapon of war—who are you, man?
notes: Historical names and epithets are transliterated rather than replaced with explanatory prose.

translation.english_text: Me? Pandiyan—the true author of Illara Jothi, who came to confront a thief of writing...
notes: The book title `இல்லற ஜோதி` is transliterated as `Illara Jothi`; the accusation `எழுத்துத் திருடன்` is retained directly.

translation.english_text: Ha...ha...ha...you are the author of Illara Jothi? Of the book?...Bravo!...Bravo!...

You took it from me saying you would have it printed, committed this dishonesty, and now you laugh to hide it, you thieves. Rather than living by stealing another man's writing, you might as well put a rope around your neck.
notes: The corrected source `அச்சியற்றுவதாக என்னிடத்திலே வாங்கி` means that the manuscript was taken on the representation that it would be printed; the earlier `unpublished writer` interpretation is discarded.

translation.english_text: Won't you leave respectfully!...
Shame...don't speak! (He slaps Paranthaman on the cheek.) Respect is for others, not for the shameless! How many of you have set out like this, living by exploiting another man's writing?
notes: The embedded slap remains inside the immutable dialogue-linked unit because it is part of that source record.

translation.english_text: A lot of them have set out like that...go away, sir.
(To the boy) Shut up, you little upstart...
notes: `முந்திரிக்கொட்டை` is rendered idiomatically as a meddling/upstart child rather than literally as `cashew nut`.

source_locator.description: Standalone action after Garudan rebukes the office boy and before PDF 15.

translation.english_text: (Paranthaman, furious, rushes to the table, opens it and takes out a revolver; Garudan stops him.)
Shh...keep quiet! Otherwise we'll have to count prison bars... Fine thing you've done...
notes: `கம்பி எண்ணனும்` is the source's colloquial jail/prison-bars expression; the earlier translation about what a youngster might think was unsupported.

source_locator.description: Standalone action after Garudan's PDF-15 rebuke and before the unlabelled coffee request.

translation.english_text: (Saying this, he takes the revolver, puts it in the drawer, closes it, and turns to the boy.)
notes: No speaker is inferred for the following source-unlabelled utterance from this action alone.

source_locator.description: Unlabelled spoken line immediately after the revolver is returned to the drawer.

translation.english_text: Hey, boy! Bring a hot cup of coffee.
notes: The booklet prints this as speech without an explicit speaker label. The English preserves it as unlabelled and does not manufacture a dialogue-record ID or speaker.

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical after the unlabelled coffee request.

translation.english_text: (The boy leaves.)
We mustn't let it go...
(Grandly) Yes, we mustn't let it go!
Hey, the fact that I was hit mustn't get out!

That's right...I told you even then not to put another man's writing out under your name—you've written the Panjanai book now! Look at the value it has...does Illara Jothi have that? Why get into needless trouble? Ah...letters have come about Panjanai...Who is that ascetic? Can we meet him? Is there a photograph? Is he a born poet or a self-made poet? Does he have a pen in his hand, or Manmatha's bow? Is there ink in the pen, or sugarcane juice? That's how they describe you. Nobody describes Illara Jothi that way. Nor does it sell very much.
notes: `பஞ்சணை` and `இல்லற ஜோதி` are retained as source book titles in transliteration.
The corrected source explicitly prints `மன்மதனின் வில்லே`; the earlier `bow in his head` rendering was an English-layer error.

translation.english_text: Even if it was not a commercial success, Illara Jothi has given me a delightful companion.
notes: The corrected Tamil reads `இன்பமான ஜோடியை` (`a delightful companion/mate`), not `ஜோதி`; the earlier English `delightful light` was based on the old erroneous reading and is superseded.

source_locator.description: Opening bracketed direction states that Bama's song has ended; the booklet prints no title or lyrics.

translation.english_text: (Bama's song has ended.)
notes: Only the source-visible performance reference is translated; no song title or lyric body is supplied or reconstructed.

source_locator.description: Opening action following the source's song-ended reference.

translation.english_text: (She takes the water pot and walks away. From the tree above, Paranthaman loops a noose around the neck of the pot and pulls it. Bama looks up—)
What kind of mischief is this...

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical after Bama's first line.

translation.english_text: (Paranthaman comes down laughing.)
The noose that fell on the pot slipped and fell around my neck,
To put a noose around your neck too.....
notes: The source's wordplay on `சுருக்கு` is retained literally so Paranthaman's next line can turn it toward the marriage cord. The scan-adjudicated Tamil `சுருக்குப் போடப் .....` breaks off after the infinitive, so the English keeps the unfinished construction rather than supplying the finite verb the earlier reading assumed.

translation.english_text: What......

Don't be afraid! Not with this rope. With a turmeric-dyed marriage cord around your emerald-jewel neck. (Bama is shy.) Bama! What I said is right, isn't it? Come on, say it...... (Bama smiles.) Ah! A breeze that subdues a storm, a block of ice that quenches a volcano—I have never even heard of such a thing!... Yet I can see that wondrous power in a single smile of yours.
notes: `மாங்கல்யக் கயிறு` is rendered as `marriage cord`; the source imagery and embedded actions remain within the immutable dialogue-linked unit.

translation.english_text: Won't all this end up as mere description?
notes: The source's `வர்ணனை` is kept as `description`; the question is not expanded into a promise absent from the Tamil.

translation.english_text: Why the doubt! (Putting a hand on her shoulder) Only yesterday he became acquainted. Today he touches and plays; are you afraid that tomorrow he may run away? Sweet-tongued one! Haven't you carefully noticed what I wrote in Illara Jothi?
notes: The corrected Tamil's sequence `நேற்று... இன்று... நாளை...` is retained explicitly. The scan-adjudicated forms `அறிமுகமானான்`, `விளையாடுகிறான்` and `ஓடிவிடுவானோ` are third person as printed and are rendered as such rather than normalised to first person; the closing `எழுதியிருக்கிறேன்` stays first person because the source prints it so. The book title remains transliterated without importing authorship claims into the speech.

translation.english_text: Will you act as you wrote?
(Wearily) Women are creatures of suspicion like this.
notes: `அலுத்தபடி` is retained as weariness/exasperation rather than strengthened into a different attitude.

translation.english_text: No...no... (turning his face toward her) Look here...
Bama! My dear! (moves closer)
No...all that only after the marriage...
But the marriage is going to happen!
Marriage. I am fortunate.

source_locator.description: Opening bracketed direction immediately after the canonical scene-7 heading.

translation.english_text: (Several women inside are busy with wedding preparations. Kumudha arrives. Poomalai eagerly runs to her—)
Kumudha!
Chinnamma! (They embrace.)
notes: The kinship address `சின்னம்மா` is transliterated rather than assigned a narrower English relationship.

translation.english_text: Why are you so late, dear?
Exams, Chinnamma. I couldn't come at once...
Sit down, Kumudha. I had thought I would marry you to my younger brother and keep you here in the household...
notes: The corrected source's `வீட்டோட இருப்பேன்னு` is retained; the historical English had dropped the household-continuity phrase.

translation.english_text: But before that, he already went and had a love marriage.
Hey, Gundumani.
notes: The corrected source label is `குண்டுமணி`; the stale `குணமணி` metadata is not retained.

source_locator.description: Standalone entrance cue before Paranthaman's first line.

translation.english_text: (Paranthaman enters.)
Ah! When did Goddess Kumudha arrive?
notes: The mock-formal `தேவி` is retained as `Goddess` to preserve Paranthaman's playful register.

translation.english_text: Uncle, you're still in full bridegroom style! Tell me, is my aunt fair or dark?
notes: `மாப்பிள்ளை முறுக்கிலேயே` is retained as a joking reference to his bridegroom swagger/style, not location.

translation.english_text: Oh dear...and an educated girl doesn't even know this! Would anyone like a woman if she were red in colour? Blood and kumkum are red—who would touch that colour? From now on, ask like this: lemon-fruit colour, jamun-fruit colour, or a mixture of the two?
notes: The source's colour-based joking and period vocabulary are translated without modernization.

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical after Paranthaman's colour joke.

translation.english_text: (Kumudha laughs.)
In the excitement of the wedding, poetry is pouring out of Uncle!
And colour poetry is pouring out too! (Laughter)
notes: The corrected source reads `கலர் கவிதைகளால்ல`; the historical `cover-poetry` rendering was based on stale text.

translation.english_text: Ask the bridegroom to come...

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical after the priest asks for the bridegroom.

translation.english_text: (Poomalai lets out a deep sigh.)
Where is the bridegroom—the auspicious hour will pass—quickly—quickly...
notes: `முகூர்த்தநேரம்` is rendered as the auspicious wedding time without adding ritual detail.

translation.english_text: Chinnamma! Uncle can't be found.
notes: The compact colloquial `மாமாவைக் காணும்` is rendered from immediate scene context without inventing a destination.

translation.english_text: Ah! Can't he be found?

source_locator.description: Closing standalone direction after Poomalai realizes the bridegroom is missing.

translation.english_text: (An uproar as they search for the bridegroom.)

source_locator.description: Opening bracketed direction immediately after the canonical scene-9 heading.

translation.english_text: (Kumudha runs to Poomalai, who is upstairs, exhausted from searching and looking as though she is in a daze.)
notes: `பிரமைபிடித்தவள்போலிருக்கும்` is kept as a dazed/disoriented appearance rather than diagnosed or intensified.

translation.english_text: Kumudha!
Chinnamma!
Kumudha! What are we to do about this disgrace... Ayyo... (she cries out)
notes: The source exclamation `அய்யோ` is retained as `Ayyo` rather than replaced with a narrower emotional interpretation.

source_locator.description: The complete source-visible content of canonical scene 10.

translation.english_text: (Water streams from Bama's eyes. The flowing water falls into her hand. The water that falls into her hand turns into a waterfall. The waterfall becomes a river.)
notes: The corrected Tamil repeats `நீர்`/`வழிந்த நீர்`; the English preserves the visual transformation without adding interpretation. Scene 10 contains no labelled dialogue.

source_locator.description: Opening boat movement in the scene-11 bracketed direction.

translation.english_text: (A boat is moving along.)

source_locator.description: The same opening direction states that Paranthaman and another woman are singing as they travel in the boat.

translation.english_text: (Paranthaman and another woman are singing as they travel in the boat.)
notes: The booklet prints only this performance reference; no song title or lyric body is supplied or reconstructed.
The source does not name the other woman, so the English does not identify her.

source_locator.description: Opening bracketed direction immediately after the canonical scene-12 heading.

translation.english_text: (Poomalai enters the house in anguish. Paranthaman is sitting there.)
Where have you come?

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical after Poomalai's first question, describing the handwritten manuscript and author name.

translation.english_text: (On the handwritten manuscript titled 'Vaazhu' that he has with him, beneath 'Vaazhu' he writes the author name 'Thuravi'.)
notes: The manuscript title `வாழு` and pen name `துறவி` are transliterated in the English derivative; the Tamil source remains authoritative.

translation.english_text: I am asking you—where have you come...
I came to my house.
You stay in your house—I will leave.
No one needs to go. I will go myself. I will die. Only then will you be at peace.
Why should you die? You still have to conduct swimming games in the flood of how many more women's tears.
Enough. After you have hinted that I ought to die, am I going to remain alive? No, no.
Don't frighten me. I know that people whose very aim in life is to roll their bodies in the mud of excitement and the mire of pleasure are afraid even to think of death.
notes: The source pairing is exactly `உற்சாகச் சேறு, உல்லாசச் சகதி`; both terms are mud/mire imagery. The historical English's `force of revelry` came from the stale misreading `சக்தி` and has been removed.

translation.english_text: So what exactly are you saying now?

Do I have to say it? The whole town is saying it! It points me out and says, 'There she is—the sister of the gambler who stole the life of a maiden who knew neither deceit nor guile.' Enough of the pain you have brought me. Father and mother must have told me a thousand times to look after my younger brother properly. I looked after you very properly indeed. Even an animal can be trained, my boy...but you simply cannot be reformed.
notes: The compressed source `சூதுவாதறியாத` is read as `சூது வாது அறியாத`—knowing neither deceit nor guile; `சூதாடி` is retained as `gambler`. The historical `reveler` / `life-dream` rendering did not match the corrected Tamil.

translation.english_text: What do you know of my situation—you will cry. The town will see it and say, 'The sister is good, the brother is bad.' Your Mukhari will win a complete victory... Your worry is that the wedding has stopped, that the many things bought for the feast have gone to waste, that the money given to the wedding-pandal man is lost, and whether the wealth already spent can ever be gathered again. But only I know the torment my mind would have suffered afterward if the Bama marriage had been completed without the money going to waste. How would you know? Are father and mother here to worry about me?
notes: `முகாரி` is retained as `Mukhari`, preserving the source's music/lament reference rather than replacing it with a different metaphor.
The corrected clause is `பணம் வீணாகாமல் பாமா பரிணயம் முடிந்திருந்தால்`; the historical English reversed its sense by saying `even if the money was wasted`.

translation.english_text: Brother, don't say things like that. Why did you run away on the wedding day?
notes: The source says `கல்யாணத்தன்று` without making it Poomalai's wedding; the historical English's `my wedding` was incorrect.

translation.english_text: Bama is not pure. I trusted her and was deceived......
That cannot be—someone has told you something false. Bama is pure gold of the finest touch.
notes: The traditional gold-quality expression `பத்தரைமாற்றுப் பசும்பொன்` is rendered by meaning rather than converted into a modern numeric assay.

translation.english_text: Not gold—brass plated with gold.
I cannot believe it. You are inventing a reason for your own fault.
(Firmly) Then don't believe it. I don't like marriage. That is all...
This enlightenment should have dawned earlier.
Even for very great men, it dawned only later. Am I ordinary...

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical after Paranthaman's enlightenment remark.

translation.english_text: (He takes the 'Vaazhu' book and leaves.)

source_locator.description: Bracketed direction introducing the lesson children near the end of scene 12.

translation.english_text: (The children who come for lessons run up to Poomalai.)
Sister, sister. Ambujam says a dog's tail cannot be straightened. Is that really true, sister?
notes: The proverb-like source line is translated literally; its placement after the preceding argument is not editorially explained.

translation.english_text: Yes. All right, come, let us study.
(Showing the Vaazhu book) Garuda! How is the book?
notes: The source book title `வாழு` is transliterated as `Vaazhu`.

translation.english_text: Absolutely splendid.
There is something very good in this book.....
What is it?
The cover, sir.
Tch! Is only the cover good? The printing too is gem-like.
notes: `அட்டை மாத்திரந்தான் நல்லா இருக்கா?` is a retort asking whether only the cover is good; it is not a suggestion to change the cover.
The source phrase `மணி மணியா` is retained as the image `gem-like` rather than normalized into a modern printing-quality term.

translation.english_text: Garuda! I did not ask for criticism of how the printing is or how the cover is; I am asking how the advice I have given is.
Ah! Do you even have to ask about that...

source_locator.description: Closing parenthetical `புத்தகத்தைப் பிரித்துப் பாடல்` after Garudan's final line.

translation.english_text: (The book is opened; a song follows.)
notes: The source does not identify a title, lyrics or performer in this line. It is therefore preserved as a direct stage/performance direction and not linked to an invented song occurrence.

source_locator.description: Opening bracketed direction states that there is a song on stage.

translation.english_text: (A song is performed on stage.)
notes: The booklet prints no title or lyric body for this stage song, so none is supplied or reconstructed.

source_locator.description: Action in the opening bracketed direction after the stage song ends.

translation.english_text: (When the song ends, Paranthaman and Garudan leave angrily.)

Comrades! Greetings! A few writers have sprung up merely to spread needless, harmful ideas in the country through obscene style and meaningless chains of phrases. Recently a book titled 'Vaazhu' has been published. Its author says that man is born into the world only for his own playful pleasures. I wrote the book 'Vaazhu Vaazha Vidu'—'Live and Let Live'—to show that both the doctrine of 'Live' and the barren philosophy of 'Do not live; life itself is illusion' are wrong. I made it into a play as well. 'Live' is selfishness. 'Do not live' is ignorance. 'Live and Let Live' is rationalism. With your support, this truth must triumph. My thanks and greetings to everyone who has come to the play.
notes: The three title/slogan forms `வாழு`, `வாழாதே`, and `வாழு வாழ விடு` are kept visibly distinct because Pandiyan's argument depends on their contrast.
`பகுத்தறிவு` is rendered as `rationalism`, preserving the source's ideological vocabulary rather than softening it to general `reason`.
The closing `அனைவருக்கும்` means everyone who came to the play; the historical English's added `dear friends` has been removed.

source_locator.description: Opening bracketed direction immediately after the canonical scene-15 heading.

translation.english_text: (There is a knock at the door. Pandiyan opens it; Punyakodi comes inside.)
Father, where had you gone?
It was all for a good matter.
notes: The corrected Tamil speaker label is exactly `புண்யகோடி`.

source_locator.description: Source-visible action after Punyakodi's first reply.

translation.english_text: (He comes inside and sits down.)
notes: The source typography around this action is irregular; it is retained as the historical scene-linked action rather than silently merged into new dialogue text.

translation.english_text: Why didn't you come to the play, father? The play was really excellent.
I heard.
Who told you, father?
All our mill workers had come, hadn't they? They told me!
The mill workers were able to come. The foreman couldn't come, could he, father?
notes: The corrected source reads `மேஸ்திரி`, meaning the mill foreman. The historical English's `superior officer` came from stale source wording and has been replaced.

translation.english_text: Don't be angry! I too had gone all the way to town on a matter concerning you......
What matter, father!
I have arranged your marriage.
Why marriage for me now? Let me first get some steady job......
The work you have is enough! A writer's work is steady work, isn't it? Look here, son! It is a very good match...and the girl is very beautiful! Don't refuse—marry her...
Shouldn't I see the girl, father?
I know all about you! That is why I brought the photograph.

source_locator.description: Standalone parenthetical after Punyakodi says he brought the photograph.

translation.english_text: (He searches the pocket of his coat.)

source_locator.description: Unlabelled spoken line immediately after the coat-pocket search; the line itself includes the photograph-giving action.

translation.english_text: What is this—does he eat one pocket with every wash? (He takes out the photograph and gives it.)
notes: This spoken line has no explicit source speaker label. It remains direct scene-linked dialogue with `speaker_label: null`; no dialogue-record ID or speaker is invented.
The complaint about a pocket being `eaten` at each wash is translated literally rather than assigning an unstated speaker or laundry subject.

translation.english_text: Well, what do you say?
As you wish.
That's the way to say it, my king! Tomorrow itself I will go to the mill owner and ask for a little money for the wedding. (Angrily) As if he is going to give it. Miser.
notes: The source closes with the separate insult `கஞ்சன்.`; it was omitted from the historical English and is restored here.

translation.english_text: I have money myself, father!
Then we can hold the wedding soon.

source_locator.description: Final standalone parenthetical after Punyakodi's last line.

translation.english_text: (Pandiyan smiles.)

source_locator.description: Opening direction: Garudan reads the wedding invitation.

translation.english_text: (Garudan is reading the wedding invitation.)

The wedding of writer Pandiyan, son of Punyakodi, foreman at Sivasakthi Mills, Singanallur, and Miss Bama of Coimbatore merchant Gunaratnam, will be celebrated grandly at the bride's residence. You and your family....
notes: The source invitation breaks off after `தங்கள் சுற்றமும்`; the English preserves that incompleteness.
The source identifies Punyakodi as Pandiyan's father but does not explicitly print a daughter-relationship word between merchant Gunaratnam and Bama, so the English does not add one.

source_locator.description: Paranthaman abruptly snatches, crumples and throws away the invitation.

translation.english_text: (Paranthaman abruptly snatches the invitation, crumples it and throws it away.)
That fellow Pandiyan keeps interfering in our affairs. The other day he staged a play and mocked our doctrine. And today, the woman we were supposed to marry....
notes: Garudan's colloquial first-person plural is retained because Paranthaman immediately interrupts and forces him to correct it in the next line.

translation.english_text: Hey....
No. The woman you were supposed to marry....
Who allowed that?
notes: The source `யார் விட்டார்கள்` is kept as a terse past/perfective challenge rather than shifted into a future prediction.

source_locator.description: Opening direction describing Bama, the approaching wedding, the knock and Paranthaman's entrance.

translation.english_text: (Bama sits like an image of sorrow, thinking of the wedding that is to take place the next day. There is a knock at the door. Bama goes and opens it. Paranthaman enters.)
Bama!

source_locator.description: Bama is startled after Paranthaman calls her.

translation.english_text: (Bama is startled.)
What is this outrage? I don't understand anything. Please go away....
Shh...don't make a noise! The people sleeping will wake up. Bama, look at me! Won't you look at me?..... Why, Bama, did you deceive me like this?...
notes: The corrected Tamil reads `என்னை இப்படி ஏமாற்றினாய்`; the earlier English `why are you changing like this` was based on a stale source reading and has been removed.

translation.english_text: Deceiving people is not my profession.

Quite right... Your lover disappeared on the wedding day. Without worrying at all about where he went or what happened to him, you hurriedly chose the next lover...an innocent who knows nothing! And I am the deceiver—isn't that it?...
Where did you go? From this world to heaven?....

Even if I had gone to heaven, I would have cast aside Tilottama who enchants there, Menaka of bewitching speech, every one of them, and leapt down from the sky thinking of your beautiful face. I went to a sorcerer's world, Bama! A sorcerer deceived me, Bama!
notes: The corrected Tamil explicitly reads `சுந்தர முகம்`, `சூனியக்கார லோகம்`, and `சூனியக்காரன்`; the stale English `conch-like face`, `world of childish fools`, and `trickster` readings are therefore removed.
Mythological names are transliterated rather than replaced.

translation.english_text: What are you saying!

Some magician...said there was a kayakalpa remedy to eat, and that if one ate it youth would not change until the age of eighty. I believed him and ate it. I thought of buying some for you too. He took me somewhere. He stole the ten thousand rupees I had and the diamond necklace I had bought for you, and disappeared somewhere.
notes: `காயகல்பம்` is retained as the traditional rejuvenation concept `kayakalpa`; the corrected Tamil explicitly prints `எண்பது வயது` (`eighty years`).

translation.english_text: Didn't you tell the police?

How could I tell the outside world of this disgrace! Broken-hearted, I wandered about and came here. And when I arrived, you had made another plan for your life...Bama! I was the one who was deceived, wasn't I? Yet you have become a greater deceiver than that magician, Bama!....
(Clutching Paranthaman's feet and sobbing) Forgive me. I could not stand up to my father's anger.
At daybreak you will be married. Another man's wife! Who am I to forgive you!
Save me. We can tell father right now and stop the wedding....
He will not stop it. There is only one way for our love to continue.
What way? (She cries.)

Don't cry! Queen of love! Ornamental sacred form of the jewel-palace of beauty! Picture that cannot be erased and redrawn—a swaying golden lamp! Kattani-pearl beauty! Eye-catching gem! If there are tears in your eyes, my heart is shaken, alas! Don't cry, Bama!.... Don't cry!
notes: The deliberately ornate sequence of endearments is preserved rather than normalized into ordinary romantic prose.
The corrected Tamil reads `அழித்தெழுதா சித்திரமே`, so the stale English `not painted even with nectar` is removed.
`கட்டாணி முத்தழகி` is kept conservatively as `Kattani-pearl beauty` rather than assigning an unsupported modern paraphrase to the source image.

translation.english_text: Tell me a way for us to live.
A way to live! We must both leave right now....
Ah!

Listen, my gold! Write a letter to your father. 'I do not like the marriage—I have left,' write that, delight of my thoughts! Graceful peacock.... Hmm, quickly...write, my dear! My unpainted portrait, write!
notes: The source's cascading endearments and imperative rhythm are retained.

source_locator.description: Opening direction describing Pandiyan's happiness and preparations outside for the bridegroom's procession.

translation.english_text: (Pandiyan is happy that he is going to marry Bama. Outside, preparations are under way for the bridegroom's procession. Inside—)
Set out quickly, son! Everything is ready.
notes: The corrected source label is exactly `புண்யகோடி`; the stale `புண்ணகோடி` metadata is removed.
`புறப்படு` is rendered as setting out/leaving, not merely getting ready.

translation.english_text: Do we need a procession, father? Somehow I don't like it.

Oh, forget that! No procession at all? Are we going to call this person and that person and arrange a concert? Can't we at least have a simple bridegroom's procession with a little ceremony? The girl isn't going to be beside you—why are you shy?
notes: The colloquial `அவாளை இவாளை` is rendered generically rather than assigned specific identities.
The corrected source label is exactly `புண்யகோடி`.

source_locator.description: The band suddenly stops; a man tells Punyakodi that the bride has run away, and Pandiyan is stunned.

translation.english_text: (The band suddenly stops. A man tells Punyakodi in his ear that the bride has run away. Pandiyan is stunned.)

source_locator.description: Opening direction: Poomalai prepares to leave town and a girl who studies under her comes to her.

translation.english_text: (Poomalai is making preparations to leave town. A girl who studies under her comes to her.)
Why are you going to the city, amma?...
notes: `அம்மா` is retained as the respectful/familiar address `amma` rather than assigning a relationship not stated by the source.

translation.english_text: Kumudha's examination result will be known in two days. I am going to bring her back.
(Coming in) Amma! Amma! Do you know what happened! The girl chosen for our young master......
notes: The corrected source label is exactly `குண்டுமணி`; the stale `குணமணி` metadata is removed.

translation.english_text: The wedding is today. What about it?
They say the girl ran away last night!
Is that so! (Thinking) Hmm...where is Paranthaman?
He...he...hmm...he was telling Garudan that he too had to go to Madras.
(Thoughtfully) Hmm...all right, get going. It's time for the train.

source_locator.description: Opening direction: Poomalai is seated in the train.

translation.english_text: (Poomalai is seated in the train.)
Amma! Then I'll get into the next carriage.
notes: The corrected source label is exactly `குண்டுமணி`; the stale `குணமணி` metadata is removed.

source_locator.description: Gundumani leaves; Pandiyan enters the same carriage; Poomalai recognizes him through his book and takes out tiffin.

translation.english_text: (He leaves. Pandiyan comes and gets into the same carriage. From the book he wrote, 'Vaazhu Vaazha Vidu,' Poomalai recognizes who he is. Then she takes out the tiffin.)
notes: The corrected Tamil says `போகிறான்`, so the stale English `She leaves` has been corrected to `He leaves`.
The Tamil book title is transliterated to preserve its connection to the earlier title contrast.

translation.english_text: Please eat....
No, thank you.
Have a little.
Many thanks! You eat!....
Which town are you going to?
Me? I don't know myself.
You are in great anguish. Such things are common in the world. You should not take them to heart.
Do you know me!...
I do...here... (She shows the book.)
(Lowering his head) What a disgrace, ayyo....
notes: The source exclamation `அய்யோ` is retained as `ayyo` rather than replaced with a more specific interpretation.

translation.english_text: Don't be distressed.
Can you understand my whole story?
(Uneasily) I understand. You, who should have been a bridegroom today......
Enough. I should never show my face to the world again!
But you have done nothing wrong.

Me? I did nothing wrong? I, who lived bound by honour and self-respect, have today become a symbol of disgrace because of my foolishness. Those who see me spit in contempt; those who have not seen me mock me. Though I had eyes I was blind, though I had ears I was deaf. Without thoroughly enquiring about a deceitful woman, I dressed myself up as a bridegroom and came running like a fool. Me? I did nothing wrong?
notes: The repeated `நானா தவறு செய்யவில்லை` is rhetorical and is preserved as a question rather than flattened into the declarative `I did nothing wrong`.
The corrected Tamil reads `கண்டவர் காரி உமிழ, காணாதவர் கேலி பேச`; the stale English `those who behold me` for `காணாதவர்` is removed.
The corrected source reads `கள்ளி யொருத்தியைப் பற்றி`; `கள்ளி` is rendered contextually as `deceitful woman` rather than the stale literalized `cactus-like woman` based on an earlier bad reading.

translation.english_text: Be quiet now. Come to Madras and take a little rest at our house.
Rest? No rest can drive away this pain.

source_locator.description: Closing direction: the train moves on.

translation.english_text: (The train moves on.)
Amma! Chinnamma is coming!
Chinnamma!
(Kumudha comes running.)
Kumudha! (They embrace.)
(Looking at Pandiyan) Chinnamma, this gentleman...
Would you know if I told you?
I know without being told. 'Vaazhu, Vaazha Vidu'—forgive me. Your name is Pandiyan, isn't it?
Yes.
Who, sir? That Pandiyan who killed Kovalan?...
Yes indeed...Soundara Pandiyan. Just look at the man!...
Come, first let's have coffee....
How many days are we to stay in a hotel? Find a house soon.
Let the house-hunting wait... Come, at least today let's go around and see the city.
Uh-uh...first we must start a family.
We will. Why are you in such a hurry? What has starting a family got to do with seeing Chennai?
What is there in Chennai?

What is there in Chennai? They tell story after story about the exhibition hall. They say the lighthouse puts even the sun to shame. Eyes that have not seen the zoo and Marina beach are sinful eyes, they say. Hmm...come! Queen of love, adorned sacred image of a jewel-beautiful palace, indelible picture. Come.
(They leave.)
notes: Source-visible standalone direction `(புறப்படுதல்)` restored as its own unit rather than folded into Paranthaman's dialogue.

translation.english_text: (A tiger in a cage.)
(To Bama) What would you do if I pushed you into the tiger's mouth?
I'd turn into grass.... Even when a tiger is hungry, it won't eat grass!
The blue sea—what a beautiful sight!
If this sea were suddenly to surge...
There is always danger beside beauty.
Many people never understand that.

(While Damayanti slept, in the middle of the night Nala deceived her, betrayed her, tore off half her sari and set off running! He went, he went, leaving that virtuous woman to suffer. He went—he went away altogether.)
notes: The corrected source narrates Nala in the third person; the historical first-person English has been removed.

translation.english_text: (In the same way, following Nala, Paranthaman goes away leaving Bama to suffer. Bama is bewildered when she cannot find Paranthaman.)
Was abandoning the beloved in the forest, in pitch darkness, not enough for the king?...
notes: The source supplies no speaker label for this closing line; none is invented. The Nala-Damayanti parallel is preserved without importing outside text.

translation.english_text: (Bama runs.)

(Bama became like a madwoman, a figure deserving pity. She ran—ran somewhere, searching for an end. The smooth tar road could not show a path to the woman who had been deceived. The beacon that guides sailors could not show direction to one who had lost all bearings. The raging sea could not compete with her heart surging in turmoil. What roared was not a tiger. The world, the world! The world in which lived the kith and kin, mother and father whom she had rejected and left behind! She could no longer face that world! She could not! She could never face it!)
notes: The source narration genuinely crosses PDF 31→32; its emphatic repetitions and the explicit sailors (`மாலுமிகள்`) reference are preserved.

translation.english_text: (She falls on the seashore.)
Gundumani! Isn't the tea ready yet?
(She comes downstairs; Poomalai comes there.)
Chinnamma! Have tea sent to him. I'm going to buy film for the camera....
(Gundumani brings the tea.)
Gundumani, wait... I'll take the tea. You go attend to your work.
All right, amma....
(Poomalai takes the tea and goes upstairs.)
notes: The subject is resolved from Poomalai's immediately preceding `நான் கொண்டுபோறேன் டீயை`; no new action is added.

translation.english_text: (To himself) When it comes to serving Pandiyan, Amma herself steps to the front—what's going on? Ah, tch, tch! Amma is a good woman...hmm...who knows? Such a... (suspiciously) what kind of... All right, all right—why should a servant concern himself with all this...
notes: The source speech is deliberately fragmentary; `அப்பேர்பட்ட ... எப்பேர்பட்ட` is not completed or reconstructed in English.

translation.english_text: (Kumudha has Pandiyan stand and takes his photograph.)
Stand properly—yes—smile a little...just a little...steady please, right...thanks....
(She takes the photograph.)
Give it here. I'll capture you.
What?...
I mean I'll take your picture.
That's what I thought! (Shyly)
(Taking the camera) Hmm...steady please....
(Kumudha stands posing like Nataraja.)
What's this!
Chinnamma!
Yes, dear!
(Poomalai arrives just then.)
notes: Unit ID preserved while its array position is restored to the source order after the two preceding calls.

translation.english_text: We've taken photos separately. The two of us will stand together—you take one!
Uh-uh, Kumudha! I don't know how to take one. You take it yourself!
Oh, Chinnamma! (Taking the camera with a pout) All right, Chinnamma! You two stand together; I'll take it. (Without guile.)
Me?
Go and stand there, Chinnamma!
(Poomalai goes and stands beside Pandiyan. Kumudha prepares to take the photograph.)
Steady please....
(Gundumani gives a joyous shout; Kumudha trembles and drops the camera.)
W...what...what?
(Showing the paper) Kumudha-amma passed! Passed! Passed!
Passed?
Passed! Kumudha, you're clever!
(They embrace.)
Kumudha, congratulations....
(The two try to shake hands.)
(Showing the newspaper) Look at this number: sixteen twenty-four....
Twenty-four.... Why, my age is twenty-four too.
My age is only sixteen.
A well-matched number indeed.
(Sharply) Hey....keep quiet....
No, ma'am. I mean Kumudha-amma should always remain sixteen years old, like Markandi.
notes: The printed proper-name form `மார்க்கண்டி` is transliterated as Markandi rather than silently normalized to a different form.

translation.english_text: (Everyone laughs.)
Then shall we leave for our town?
You don't have to worry about him, amma. From now on, even if we chase him away, he won't leave us!
(Paranthaman arrives.)
Come, man! The last two or three weeks must have been one grand, jolly life....
Poor thing...Bama longed to set up a family in Chennai and put me in the prison of domestic life... Where she went, what happened to her!....
Hmm...family life and all that—man ought to be free, like me. Hasn't God created an example for us—the one that flits from flower to flower......
notes: The source leaves the flower-to-flower comparison unfinished; the historical English insertion of `bee` has been removed.

translation.english_text: The monkey that leaps from tree to tree.
Hey....
I thought you had forgotten, so I reminded you.
Kambar's son Ambikapathi! Keep quiet, you meddlesome little cashew nut!
(The sound of a workers' procession passing along the street is heard.)
Slogan
notes: Structural heading `கோஷம்`; retained separately from the chant body.

translation.english_text: Raise the wages of the Sivasakthi Mill workers. Raise the workers' wages...raise the workers' wages.
notes: The source labels this standalone block `கோஷம்`; no individual speaker is invented.

translation.english_text: What's that?
It has nothing to do with us.
Not to us—to us! Tell the matter including him too, you donkey!
notes: The compressed colloquial `நமக்காமில்ல நமக்கு! இவரும் சேந்துக்கிறாரு` is kept deliberately close to the source rather than expanded into a different explanation.

translation.english_text: The mill workers are agitating for a wage increase!...
Is that so? Then it has nothing to do with us.
Why not? I've got an idea. If we make use of this agitation and write a book about the toilers, it will sell well at a time like this.
Yes....I'll start writing today itself. What shall we call the book...ah...right.... 'The Toiler's Voice.'
Bravo! 'The Toiler's Voice.' What a brain! What a brain!
First pay a little attention to my voice!
What is it?
My wages.
(Angrily) Hey! If a book is written for the mill workers...
I'm a worker too, sir!...
A great worker he is! Paranthama! You start writing! Of the profit, one quarter for you and three quarters for me.
For me...
A slap! (He slaps him.)
(The boy cries.)
notes: Restores the source-visible opening `(பையன் அழுதல்)`. The historical scene-29 copy of this action was removed; it belongs to canonical scene 30.

translation.english_text: (Bama's father, Gunarathnam, is sorrowfully telling Poomalai about his daughter.)
Was it only she who went? She mortgaged the house and went off with the thousand rupees' worth of jewellery I'd had made too!
It's only a thousand rupees' worth of jewellery, isn't it? Here.... (Removing her own ornaments and handing them over) Keep these. (She gives them.)
(Taking them) Why? Whom am I going to adorn with these and admire? You keep them yourself. (Throwing them down) Those who betrayed me will come to ruin!...
(He leaves. Poomalai sits wearily on the sofa. Paranthaman comes in and sees the jewellery lying on the floor.)
Akka, where did this jewellery come from?
(Poomalai is silent.)
Why is it lying down here like this? (He picks it up.) These are all gold ornaments, aren't they?
No. The smile of betrayal!
notes: The source makes a wordplay between `பொன்னகை` (gold ornament) and `புன்னகை` (smile); the English preserves the semantic turn, though not the Tamil sound-play.

translation.english_text: (As if he does not understand) What's this! What's the matter, akka?
A tiger cannot live long in a deerskin, Paranthama! A hunter will come to hunt it too. People do not leave alive those who toy with the women of the town!... Remember that!
Every time I come home, is it this same lament? Looks as though a man can't live in peace at all!
A man must not live only for himself. He must let others live too!
All right, enough, enough. I suppose I should put on saffron robes and disappear somewhere.

Why! Do you think you can deceive people easily behind that screen? Madman who has regarded womankind as a swarm of worms writhing in the earth! Where did Bama go? Tell me. Where did you leave her to suffer? What became of that poor young girl who came to play on a volcano? Tell me! Won't you tell me, sinner! Where is Bama?
Go and look for her in the other world!
(He leaves.)
(Tears welling) Ah! Amma! Appa! It seems I will not be able to keep the promise I gave you!
(Pandiyan sits absorbed in thought, continuing to write. Kumudha sings ‘Pandiyan, en sollai’ [‘Pandiyan, my word...’], openly expressing her love through expressive gestures.)
notes: Only the song reference/title fragment printed in the booklet is translated; absent lyrics are not reconstructed.

translation.english_text: I have never gone against your word!
Pandiyan!
(They embrace.)
(A labourer who has carried in a bale of paper speaks angrily.)
I've carried such a huge load all this way. Pay me properly....
Eight annas, that's all. Take it and leave respectfully! Nonsense....
What, sir? You're a big man, yet you use such petty words. ‘Nonsense,’ is it?....
(Paranthaman strikes him hard two or three times.)
Don't hit me, sir. I am a worker!
Worker. A worker, he says—a worker....
(The labourer runs outside.)
If they won't take the money they're given, these fellows all need to be kicked like this.
(They look at the office boy; he stands covering his mouth.)
‘The Voice of the Toiler’! Garuda! The title has turned out well, hasn't it? (Leafing through the book.)
Not just the title! Five thousand copies sold in two days! What more do we need?
(Paranthaman lights a cigarette. ‘The Voice of the Toiler’ lies on the table. Punyakodi enters.)
Who are you?
Don't you know me? I am the labour leader. You know why I've come....
What is it, sir?....
(Garudan and Paranthaman become alert.)
If a worker asks for higher wages, that ought to be considered....
No, sir, he wasn't asking for wages. He carried this paper bale here....
Not him! I mean the mill worker.
Yes, yes. Employers who ignore workers' problems must not be spared.
Garuda! What use is shouting with our mouths? If the voice of the toilers is to gain strength, we must launch a great agitation....
That's the way to speak....

The toilers are the backbone of this country. The working class is the very life of a nation. We must not let it become dispirited! I have taken a solemn vow. We must soon begin the struggle for workers' liberation.

Bravo! Bravo! If there are truly resolute young men like you, liberation will dawn for the whole world in a single day. Reading your ‘The Voice of the Toiler’ turns even a decrepit old man into a youth, and a coward into a tiger. You must preside over tomorrow's public meeting.
Preside? Me? No, I am a servant of the public.
No, brother! Don't say that! Thousands of workers want it too.
Workers are my comrades! I shall fulfil their loving command. From now on, everything the worker desires must happen in this world.
Yes...yes....
(The office boy holds out his hand to Garudan.)
A higher salary....
Shoo, get lost! We're discussing great matters of the world....
Then I'll be going, sir....
Namaskaram.
(To Garudan) I'll be going, sir!
(Thousands of workers, with a police guard present, wait for Paranthaman's speech.)

Brothers! Leader Paranthaman, whom all of us have been eagerly awaiting, will arrive shortly. Everyone remain calm! Many revolutionary plans are to be carried out today. We are not going to fear anyone. No fear, no fear—even if the whole world opposes us, no fear.
Yes, yes....

(A sudden explosive sound sends the crowd scattering in confusion. Then an old Austin arrives, Garudan driving and Paranthaman seated inside. It becomes clear that the car's exhaust made the sound. They take their places on the platform and the crowd settles.)

The golden son of the toilers, the fearless lion whom we have watched the road and eagerly awaited—Paranthaman—has graced this union to remove our distress. I request that this garland be placed upon him and that he preside.
(To a man) Hey...you second it!
(Trembling) I se...se...second Paranthaman presiding.
You really ‘seconded’ it well!
notes: Garudan jokes on the stammered Tamil ஆ...மோதிக்கிறேன் / மோதிக்கிட்டீங்க; the exact sound-play is not reproducible in English.

translation.english_text: (He is garlanded; applause. Paranthaman begins speaking without removing the garland.)

Mr Chairman! (The people laugh.) Oh! I am the chairman, am I? Forgive me. My aim is that the broken-hearted toiler who clears forest, prepares the field, drives the cattle in the morning, takes up the plough and returns home in the evening—and the mill worker who turns blood into pools of sweat, weary in spirit and labouring day after day—should gain a brand-new life.... When the poor say they are hungry, I feel as though my heart will burst. When they shed tears, all my blood boils. To crush the arrogance of those who refuse our demands—an immediate strike! We must set out as one united mass! Victory is ours! Victory is ours!
Name two people who said there should be no violence against living beings.
Buddha, Gandhi.
Mukunda! Who are the Three Crowned Kings?
The Chera, the Chola.... (Hesitates.)
Hmm. Say it.
(At the word ‘Pandiyan,’ her expression changes and her lips murmur. Then, to the students:)
All right, go home and come back tomorrow.
(She sends everyone away.)
(After they leave, she goes toward the garden.)
(Cheers. Punyakodi is overflowing with delight.)
notes: This source-visible action is printed at the beginning of scene 34; the historical English layer had incorrectly attached it to scene 33.

translation.english_text: (Poomalai is with the children.)
Pandiyan.
notes: The source prints this answer without a speaker label. It is retained as source-visible unlabelled speech; no dialogue-record ID or speaker is invented.

translation.english_text: (Poomalai approaches Pandiyan, who is enjoying nature.)
I hope I'm not disturbing your thoughts....
No, no....
To what have you lost your heart? To the beauty of the sky—or the movement of the clouds?
In the mature grove that dwells in silence, delighting with song....
notes: The source line is syntactically incomplete and is preserved as an unfinished poetic utterance.

translation.english_text: Are you yearning for the skylark's arrival? Pandiyan! Realising that the smiling jasmine and charming grove are not enough to feast your thoughts, the skylark itself has flown here!
Where?
It isn't visible. It can be seen with the eyes too. But first you must try to see it with the heart.
(Suspiciously) Poomalai......
(As he speaks, she hears a voice call ‘Akka!’ and turns with a start. Paranthaman enters.)
Who is he?
Paranthama, this is....
Don't tell me; I know. Who let this scoundrel into the house?
(Angrily) Paranthama....
Don't snap at me! What you've done is actually a good thing! I've been searching for him for many days.
Why are you looking for me?
Ah! To give you a gift. Here—take this, one in return for the other!
(He slaps Pandiyan. Kumudha, who has arrived there, slaps Paranthaman across the cheek.)
Ah...what!...Kumudha!
Fool!
(Slapping Kumudha) Tch! Shut your mouth.
(She slaps her several times.)
Chinnamma! Chinnamma!
(She runs inside sobbing uncontrollably. Paranthaman leaves in fury. Pandiyan stands stunned, then slowly moves away.)
My life is an arena of contests!....
(Kumudha is crying.)
Don't cry, Kumudha! (Distressed)
Chinnamma! Why did you hit me, Chinnamma? I haven't done anything wrong, Chinnamma!
Who is Paranthaman? Isn't he one of us too? How could you go and hit him?
Chinnamma, is uncle allowed to treat Pandiyan like that?
I'm here to question that! Right in front of me, he....
notes: The corrected source utterance is unfinished at the page break; the English preserves the incompleteness instead of supplying a missing action.

translation.english_text: Your younger brother matters more to you!
And to you?
My lover matters more to me!
(Startled) Lover?....
Yes! Pandiyan is my lover!
Your lover?
(Sobbing, Poomalai goes aside and cries in despair. Kumudha runs to her.)
Am I not allowed to love?
Has he given his consent?
Our two hearts have become one!
Tch! What a great mistake I've made, Kumudha!
What mistake did you make, Chinnamma? Was bringing him here the mistake? Or was introducing him to me the mistake?
There was no mistake in bringing him. Nor in introducing him.
Then was it wrong that I showed him affection?
Not that either, Kumudha! The mistake was that a plant tried to climb the branch on which a creeper was already spreading.
notes: The source's creeper/plant metaphor is preserved rather than replaced with an explicit explanation of the romantic triangle.

translation.english_text: I don't understand....
You need not understand; you must never understand.
Chinnamma! Won't you permit our love?
I permit it, dear! I bless both of you this very moment....Pandiyan! Pandiyan!
(She leaves.)
notes: The corrected source prints this carry-over action at the beginning of scene 37. The historical English layer had incorrectly placed it at the end of scene 36.

translation.english_text: (Punyakodi hands strike notices to the boy.)
They must be pasted all over town overnight! Not a single wall should be left! Understand?
Yes, sir!...
All right, go!
(The boy leaves. Pandiyan enters. Seeing Pandiyan's sorrowful face, Punyakodi comes near him.)
What is it, son? Why are you sad?
Nothing, father!
You were happy all through yesterday! What is it again now?
I have no worries.
Hmm...Pandiyan! There was something I wanted to tell you!...hmm....
(A little startled) What is it, father?
That...that....
(He shows him a photograph of a woman.)
Look at this!
(Looking at the picture) Father! I don't want marriage at all!
All right, you don't want it...but this girl....
Whoever she is, I don't need it.
Why are you in such a hurry, son? That girl is desperately longing!
Let her long! So what?
I'm saying the girl is willing.
Oh no, what trouble is this!...
There's no trouble...people in town will shout that an old man shouldn't marry...that's why I'm telling you all this.
I don't want marriage now! I won't want marriage even when I'm old!
Hey, not for you, not for you! Forget that! I'm talking about myself!
Father! The marriage is for you?
Why are you surprised? Is this the eighth wonder of the world?
When did this desire come to you, father?
Yes, boy! What a fine question! When did desire come, you ask? As though I have written down the year, month and date. You're asking for the horoscope of desire.
Even if desire has no horoscope, there is a horoscope to prove that you have crossed sixty, father!
Impertinent fellow!
Father! Don't ruin a young woman's life!
Fool! I'm going to give a young woman a life! Don't rave without understanding! No one will marry this girl. She is mute!
This mad society turns even women who can speak into silent women; would it leave mute women alive?
So what do you say now?
I ask you to change your decision.
Impossible! You are the one who must change your decision. I was born before you!
Who denies it! You're at the age to fondle grandchildren!
After I brought you into the world, raised and protected you, and made you a man, is this how you should talk back to me?

For that I offer you a thousand salutations. But at the age when you should be handing over the garland at your son's wedding, you say you will become the bridegroom yourself; I can never permit that!
Bah! Who are you to permit me? I'll do as I please.
Don't do it, father—don't make this disastrous decision!
Bah! Don't speak to me!
Your marriage?
I'm going through with it.
Have you come to hate me?
I'll drive you out.
You don't have to drive me out. I'll go myself.
Get out! Don't show your face to me again! Go!
I'm going. May your intoxication clear soon. (He leaves.)
Go on, go! 'May your intoxication clear,' he says. As though I'm sitting here drunk!
notes: The source plays on Pandiyan's figurative `போதை` and Punyakodi's literal retort about drinking; the contrast is preserved explicitly.

translation.english_text: (Pandiyan walks in confusion; only his voice is heard over his face.)

On the wedding day, one woman deceived me. Two women are competing for love. The bedchamber of an old man who walks leaning on a staff is becoming a sacrificial rock for a woman. A women's world filled with both comedy and pain!
(Pandiyan meets Poomalai. He stops with a start.)
Poomalai!
(Choked with emotion) Forgive me!...I disturbed your mind.
You are the one who must forgive me! I was the cause of the dark spot called love appearing in your pure white heart!...
Love is not a dark spot. Are unreachable grapes sour, Pandiyan? (In pain) Kumudha is the one who captured your heart! Accept her!
My life is an arena of contests! An earthquake! Gardens like Kumudha should not be caught in it and ruined!....
It is no longer an arena of contests. Poomalai has admitted defeat. So it is no earthquake either; it is a breeze carrying a new fragrance—Kumudha is calling you, and so....
(Sadly) Poomalai....
(With sorrowful resolve) Pandiyan, I have sacrificed my love—for my Kumudha!
Are you alone entitled to sacrifice love? I have that right too.
No—accept my Kumudha! Don't deceive her! She does not have the strength to carry sorrow! I plead with you. Forget my mistakes! Come home!
Poomalai....
I'm inviting you happily! Wipe the tears of my precious Kumudha! It is enough for me if she lives! Come....
(Pandiyan walks with her.)
notes: The corrected source prints this carry-over action at the beginning of scene 39. The historical English layer had incorrectly placed it at the end of scene 38.

translation.english_text: (Mill-strike posters have been pasted on walls throughout the town.)
(Inside the mill owner's room.)
(Paranthaman and Garudan arrive.)
Come....sit down!....
(The two remain standing.)
Why did you call us?
(The two sit down.)
Hmm...about this strike....
It is all my arrangement—thousands of workers are ready to follow the path I showed them.
Mr Paranthaman! I know that only you can stop the mill workers' agitation.
Any doubt about that! If not for Paranthaman, by now they would have destroyed the mill itself!
And they were even about to endanger your life! I was the one who stopped them!
I'm pleased! Many thanks for saving my life! As a small token of help from me, I offer you these five thousand rupees.
What...money?
Take it! We can add it to the workers' fund! After all, we were born only to labour for the poor!
I am not giving this thinking of it as a bribe.
And I am not accepting it thinking of it that way either.
If you can somehow stop this strike.....
It can be stopped. But that is possible only if Punyakodi is won over!
Punyakodi....he'll ask for at least three thousand!
I'll give it! I'll give it right now.
(He takes out the money and gives it.)
For the sake of your good nature, and because I want our friendship to continue, I am giving up a major agitation.
Many thanks!

(Standing up in the car) Dear workers! Our struggle has succeeded! The owner has trembled before our agitation!... He has assured me that very soon he will attend to the question of a wage increase! Warriors! We have won!
For our leader Paranthaman!
Jai! Jai!
Therefore, as your leader, I ask all of you to return peacefully to work. We will soon celebrate our victory in grand fashion.
(The scene ends amid slogans of 'Jai to Paranthaman!')
(The two rise.)
notes: The corrected source prints this carry-over action at the beginning of scene 40. The historical English layer had incorrectly placed it at the end of scene 39.

translation.english_text: (Paranthaman enters, removes his coat and hangs it on the stand, then goes upstairs. As he climbs, he throws away his cigarette; it falls into the pocket of the hanging coat. The pocket begins to smoke. Poomalai, passing that way, sees the coat catching fire, runs to it and puts it out. In the coat pocket she finds the bundle of notes received from the mill owner, sealed 'Sivasakthi Mills,' and her expression changes. In the same pocket is a small slip.)
notes: This single bracketed source direction crosses PDF 52→53 and is retained as one cross-page translation unit.

translation.english_text:
Kalyani ... 1000
Subathra ... 300
Sulochana ... 500
Devaki ... 1200
notes: The four-name amount list is printed on the slip found in Paranthaman's coat.

translation.english_text: (Poomalai takes these and goes inside. Pandiyan arrives holding a newspaper, comes into the hall, sits down and reads.)
SIVASAKTHI MILL STRIKE ENDED. WORKERS RETURNED TO WORK.
notes: Translated from the bold newspaper headline explicitly quoted in the scene.

translation.english_text: (Pandiyan reads the bold headline carefully. Paranthaman comes downstairs, looks at his coat and finds the money missing. He goes to Pandiyan, who is reading, and feels around Pandiyan's pocket searching for it.)
What are you looking for?
Money....
Ask me; I'll give you some....
(Pandiyan takes out a ten-rupee note and gives it to him.)
(Laughing mockingly) What a fine thief! Are you going to give me the money properly or not?...
What are you saying now?
Hey! So that's it. You've started stealing even inside the house! Even I don't steal at home.
(He hears a voice call 'Paranthama,' turns, and Poomalai enters.)
What is it?
Look, Akka. I had some money; he stole it.
Which money?
I brought it from the publishing office.
I know where you brought it from.
That's the truth, Akka!

Look, it has a seal on it. You thundered, 'For the toiling worker with a backbone, is Mukhari the enchanting song?' Look—the seal says this is money the mill owner gave you as a reward for that thunderous slogan!
notes: `முகாரி` is retained as Mukhari rather than replaced by an inferred emotional gloss.

translation.english_text: (She shows the bundle of money. The Sivasakthi Mill seal is clearly visible.)
Oh.... so he stole the money and gave it to you?
Enough! After acting as a blackleg, betraying the poor and taking a payoff, you still have the nerve to speak.
Akka! You don't know why I took it. It was to add it to the workers' welfare fund!
I read that too.... Look here. One thousand for Kalyani, three hundred for Subathra, five hundred for Sulochana, one thousand two hundred for Devaki.

(Trying to manage the situation) Ha ha ha—oh, oh, did you misunderstand that? Ayyo, Rama, Muruga! Garudan and I are going to open a cinema theatre. Kalyani, Subathra, Sulochana, Devaki—this is the account of advances paid to release all those films there! Ha ha ha, ayyo, ayyo.
(He picks up the money and the slip that Poomalai placed on the table. His mocking laughter turns to anger and, in the same action, he turns to Pandiyan.)
Hey, you're the cause of all this.
The cause of what? Of your taking a bribe, or of betraying the workers?
Speak respectfully!
(Kumudha comes in.)
You should learn that yourself, Uncle!
(She comes and stands beside Pandiyan. Realising the situation may worsen, Poomalai turns to Kumudha.)
Kumudha! Take him inside, dear!
(Pandiyan turns to go inside with Kumudha.)
Yes! Take him inside, sing 'Aararo,' and lull the baby to sleep!
(Angrily) Enough!
(Sharply) Kumudha!
(Kumudha leaves with Pandiyan.)
notes: Source-visible direction recovered during corrected-source reconciliation; a new unit ID is used so historical translation-unit IDs remain stable.

translation.english_text: I can't tell whether this is a house or a brothel!
Paranthama! Speak calmly!
Then what? Is it proper to let an unmarried girl go around with some good-for-nothing fellow?
She is married. Pandiyan and Kumudha are husband and wife.
A Gandharva marriage—or did you dream it up?
A registered marriage.
A registered marriage. I am here—there is still a man in this house. A registered marriage without my knowing....
notes: The source syntax and punctuation are irregular here; the English retains the broken, indignant delivery rather than smoothing it into a new sentence.

translation.english_text: You live in this house? At least the word 'house' has come from your mouth—that alone makes me happy!...
notes: Recovered explicitly labelled source utterance; new translation unit added without renumbering historical translation-unit IDs.

translation.english_text: Akka! I understand you now. I understand that all the affection you showed, calling me 'little brother, little brother,' was mere pretence. Otherwise, after telling me as though affection overflowed, 'Kumudha lives for you; she is your wife,' would you now say that you have made her the wife of some orphaned fellow!
notes: Recovered explicitly labelled source utterance; new translation unit added without renumbering historical translation-unit IDs.

translation.english_text: Why do you need a wife? Whenever you wish, wives are available to you! For those beauties who ask for wealth without asking for love, there are innocent workers to pawn to the mill owner so that you can lavish money on them...
notes: This labelled utterance crosses PDF 56→57 and remains one translation unit.
Corrected-source reconciliation replaces the historical mistranscription of `அன்பைக் கேட்- / காமல் ஐஸ்வரியத்தைக் கேட்கும்` while preserving the genuine physical page split.

translation.english_text: Enough, stop!
Intelligent! Pure! I expected praises like these to come to you. I never imagined words of blame like 'debauchee' and 'wrongdoer' would come instead.
(Paranthaman leaves. Poomalai stands there, distressed, watching him go.)
(Pandiyan is rapidly writing page after page. Kumudha comes near eagerly and watches.)
Why have you suddenly started writing?
I found a good situation; I'm writing a song.
For which magazine?
Which magazine would I write for....
Well then, let's hear the song.
(Pandiyan sings what he has written.)
“Kalappadam, kalappadam” [“Adulteration, adulteration”]
notes: Only the repeated title/refrain printed in the booklet is translated. No missing lyric lines are imported or reconstructed.

translation.english_text: (The office boy sings the song ‘Kalappadam’.)
notes: This is the source-explicit reprise of the named song. The booklet prints no additional lyrics here.

translation.english_text: (Paranthaman comes, takes the periodical from the boy and tears it up. His lips alone mutter ‘Pandiyan’ in anger.)
notes: The source narrates the muttered name within prose rather than as a separately labelled dialogue line; no speaker-labelled dialogue record is invented.

translation.english_text: (At the grounds, Garudan stands at a distance watching the gathering. Pandiyan is speaking.)

Comrades! A few traitors have set out claiming that they are serving the suffering working class. Workers are a beautiful garland woven from the flowers of enthusiasm. Do not put it around a monkey's neck merely to admire it. Do not trust a false leader who mortgages your feeling, your rights, your enthusiasm and your fervour in order to earn name, fame and money.
(Garudan becomes angry.)

I am no coward who says there should be no struggle. Those who incite you to struggle are not tigers; they are cats seeking fame. I say this only to warn you.... No rational person will reject a non-violent liberation struggle. But an agitation without a foundation will fall like a tall tree without roots. Pomp, newspaper publicity, cries of 'Jai' to Paranthaman—these displays cannot make anyone the leader of the toilers.
notes: This speech appears after the Garudan-reaction direction without a renewed speaker label. It is therefore preserved as source-unlabelled direct speech with no invented dialogue-record ID, despite the surrounding context indicating continuation of the platform speech.

translation.english_text: (Applause.)
(Garudan leaves angrily.)
(The mill owner and Usha.)
I heaved a sigh of relief thinking one fellow was gone. Now another one sprouts up—Pandiyan.
Can you think everyone is like Paranthaman and knock them down with money? People firm in their ideals will not bow their heads before the safe, Appa!
Keep quiet, Usha! You don't know anything!
What, Appa? Is it your opinion that a lady doctor knows nothing about the world?
Lady doctor!... These workers keep tormenting me with 'workers, workers' and cause me losses running into thousands. Can you give medicine for that mental anguish?

Oh! I can. But this medicine must be placed on the leaf called the heart, mixed with the honey called compassion, and taken. Do you know the name of the medicine, Appa? Egalitarianism. Equality. It will taste a little bitter at first. Then it will become all right.
Usha!
Why are you getting angry? Attend to the workers' grievances. Everything will settle down.
(The peon enters.)
It's Pandiyan. He has come to see you.
Pandiyan! Tell him to come! Tell him to come! Did you see, Usha? These fellows put on the costume of leaders only to hunt for money.
(Pandiyan enters.)
(Sitting down) I came about an important matter....
Tell me....
The workers.
I know. Ask for however much money you want to suppress them; I'll give it.
Sir! I am not Paranthaman, who thunders, 'The owner on the bed—the toiler in famine,' and then swims in bribes. I am Pandiyan—a comrade of the toilers....
notes: This source-labelled utterance crosses PDF 59→60 and remains one English unit.
The Tamil deliberately plays on `மஞ்சம் / பஞ்சம் / லஞ்சம்`; the semantic contrast is preserved, but the exact sound pattern cannot be reproduced naturally in English.

translation.english_text: Pandiyan, listen to me.
I need not listen to your words. You pay attention to the sighs of those who labour!
Sighs, labour, sweat, blood—I've heard all this so much that my ears are blocked!

Your ears will become blocked, your eyes will go dark, your mouth will close. Your hands and legs will not move! In the end, even your heart will stop. I am warning you so that such a pitiable state does not come about.
Hey, did you come here to deliver a sermon?
